newsitem.title: USA: Cirrus Logic reports big loss, to lay off 400 workers.
newsitem.headline: Cirrus Logic reports big loss, to lay off 400 workers.

text.p: Cirrus Logic Inc. reported a big, unexpected loss Wednesday for its fiscal fourth quarter, and said it plans to lay off 400 people, or 15 percent of its employees.
Cirrus, a maker of computer chips to handle graphics and sound, also reshuffled its management to make day-to-day operations more efficient.
Cirrus, which has been slow to introduce up-to-date 3-D graphics chips for the latest personal computers, blamed the loss on weak sales of existing products.
The Fremont, Calif.-based company reported a fourth-quarter loss from operations, excluding charges, of $1.5 million, or 2 cents a share for the quarter ended March 29.

With a $55.5 million charge for the restructuring and inventory adjustments, Cirrus reported a total loss of $51.6 million, or 79 cents a share. In the same quarter a year ago, the company had a loss of $88.4 million, or $1.38 a share.
Wall Street expected Cirrus to earn a profit of 8 cents a share, according to a recent analyst survey by Zacks Investment Research.
Revenue fell 8.6 percent to $212.9 million from $233.1 million a year ago.

In the past year, Cirrus' revenue has dropped because it underestimated demand for 3-D graphic chips -- the electronic components that speed up a personal computer's ability to display realistic animation and graphics.

Meanwhile, Intel Corp., the world's biggest computer chipmaker, has been making its Pentium microprocessors better at handling the PC's basic graphic funtions, eliminating the need for some of the seperate graphic chips from companies such as Cirrus.
Cirrus gets about a quarter of its revenue from sale of electronic components for PCs. It also makes components for telecommunication gear and other computer equipment.
"Our recovery has proceeded slower than expected," said company Chief Executive Michael Hackworth.
To cut costs, the company said it would fire 400 of its employees.
Cirrus also named Thomas Kelly, formerly the chief financial officer, as chief operating officer. Ron Shelton, the former vice president of finance, will replace Kelly as CFO.

Cirrus had one bright spot. The company said revenue from components to run computer disk drives rose 32 percent from the prior quarter. Cirrus gets about 30 percent of its revenue from these products.
